extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers interested in scientific method and generalisation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on forming and testing generalisations in the physical sciences, emphasizing the Law of Continuity, the use of extreme and low-intensity instances, detection of continuity across phenomena, and cautions/limits when extrapolating from observed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities are matters of degree, not absolutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities variable in degree will be found in every substance in a greater or less degree; we are learning that there are no substances absolutely opaque, non-conducting, non-electric, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat putatively absent properties as matters of intensity rather than strict absence; re-evaluate rules (e.g., Newton's rule about universal qualities) that assume absolute presence/absence. Examples discussed: magnetism (including diamagnetism), opacity, conductivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of extreme (ostensive/predominant) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme or conspicuous instances (Ostensive, Light-giving, Free and Predominant Instances) show the nature under investigation 'naked' or in its highest degree and are historically and experimentally valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use materials with pronounced properties to reveal phenomena and facilitate experiments. Historical examples: loadstone (magnetism), amber (frictional electricity), Iceland spar (double refraction), quicksilver as ostensive instance of density. Bacon's terminology and endorsement are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of extremely low (clandestine) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Clandestine Instances exhibit a nature in the least intensity, in a rudimentary state, and can be important for detecting causes by difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek and study low-degree manifestations of phenomena as they can be as informative as extreme cases. Examples: hydrogen's minimal density/atomic weight, liquefied nitrous oxide's low refractive index, strontium compounds' low dispersive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose materials with pre-eminent properties for experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain substances possess powers pre-eminent for special experimental purposes and are therefore invaluable (e.g., rock-salt for diathermancy, quartz for UV transparency, diamond for high refractive index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit such materials to detect subtle effects (e.g., Faraday discovered magneto-optic rotation using heavy glass). Listing of useful substances: rock-salt, quartz, lead glass, diamond, cinnabar, copper, iron, bismuth, cyanite, sodium, and water with its extreme qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting continuity: beware differing appearances from similar causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomena of closely similar or identical nature may present very different appearances because of extreme differences of degree or magnitude; without careful analysis one may widely separate facts/processes that are really the same law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze underlying changes and consider degree/magnitude before asserting distinct laws. Examples: gradual rusting vs rapid combustion, lightning vs gentle current, cloud particle suspension, microscopic oscillatory motion of suspended particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and intensity can radically change observable behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Masses of very different size or processes of very different intensity may show apparent behavioral differences arising from intensity of forces; extreme slowness or minuteness can disguise continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for scaling effects (mass, particle size, intensity, time) when comparing cases. Examples: iron divided into fine particles combusts readily; cloud particles fall too slowly to be noticed; enormous ratio differences between lightning and battery discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Law of Continuity (Natura non agit per saltum)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is true of one case will be true of similar cases and probably true of probably similar cases; when a law holds up to a point, expect it to continue a little further—continuity underlies many inductive inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuity as a principle for extrapolation: the longer/closer the observed experience, the stronger the inference; extrapolation over greater time/space reduces probability. Examples: predicting uniform motion from observed near-uniform motion (Galileo), inferring unseen parts of a circle from visible arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight the Law of Continuity differently by domain
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of continuity carries more weight in exact physical laws (those ultimately resting on simple laws of motion) than in less exact domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply continuity cautiously outside domains where precise physical laws hold; in complex or less exact phenomena the principle may often be wrong as well as right. Example: astronomers' previous assumption that all nebulae would be resolvable was overturned by spectroscopic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions and failures in applying the Law of Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle may appear to fail for three main reasons: (1) imperfect observation may hide forewarnings of change, (2) complex mathematical laws may show singular points that produce abrupt effects, (3) true discontinuities may occur when independent causes intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before rejecting continuity, consider measurement limits (e.g., ice-water transition shows forewarning if measured precisely); recognize mathematical singularities (e.g., total internal reflection has no discontinuity in wave theory); accept genuine discontinuities where external causes arise (e.g., earthquakes causing tidal anomalies, meteoric stones). Examples: ice fusion, Faraday's initial overgeneralisation about magnetism (negative magnetism), gravity inside a shell showing discontinuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forewarning principle: look for infinitesimal indicators of impending change
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent abrupt changes often have small indications detectable by precise measurement; continuous curves with rapid flexures replace angular, abrupt descriptions if observed accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for small deviations from simple laws (e.g., Boyle, Dalton) as forewarnings of phase changes or law breakdowns; use increasingly precise measurement to reveal gradual transitions (e.g., ice warming behaviour near melting point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use continuity to construct negative (impossibility) arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments based on continuity can show a hypothesis impossible if it implies an infinite regress or requires an arbitrary breach of continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ continuity to refute theories that entail endless repetition or logically absurd nesting (example: Bonnet's preformation theory of reproduction is refuted by the implication of nested germs ad infinitum, illustrated by Henry Baker's poem). Use such arguments to exclude implausible causal schemes.
